try hard not think about the trauma

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette:
Harold is a 77-year-old white American man who has worked as a delivery driver for most of his adult life, a job he has held well into his eighth decade partly out of financial necessity and partly because the routine of it - the familiar routes, the small talk at doorsteps, the sense of being useful - had always suited his temperament. He is married, and by his own account his wife has been his steadiest anchor. He came to the clinic several months after being assaulted during an evening delivery run, and the distance between that night and his first appointment was filled with a kind of private struggle he had not told anyone about in full.

It happened in early autumn, on a residential street he had driven dozens of times. He had stepped out of his van with a package when two men approached him from behind a parked car. What followed was brief but brutal - he was shoved hard against the side of his vehicle, punched twice in the face, and had his wallet and phone taken before the men ran. He was left on the ground, disoriented, blood from a cut above his eye running into his collar. A neighbor eventually called for help. The whole incident lasted perhaps ninety seconds, but in those ninety seconds something shifted in Harold's understanding of the world that has not shifted back.

In the weeks that followed, Harold found that the world he thought he knew - one in which a man doing honest work on a familiar street was essentially safe, in which the ordinary social contract held - had simply stopped making sense to him. He had believed, without ever articulating it, that a certain kind of life earned a certain kind of protection. That belief was gone, and in its place was something closer to bewilderment. He had come to feel that he could not trust his own judgment in situations that had once seemed straightforward. He replays small decisions from that evening - why did he park where he did, why did he not see them sooner - and each replay leaves him less certain of himself rather than more. What frightened him most was not the physical injury, which healed, but the suspicion that he was no longer a reliable reader of situations, that his instincts had failed him when they mattered.

Harold returned to work within two weeks, which surprised his wife, though she did not press him on it. What she did not know was that staying busy was the closest thing to relief he had found. On his route, he keeps the radio loud and moves quickly between stops. When the van slows near any parked car on a residential street, particularly in the late afternoon when the light begins to drop, his body tightens and his eyes sweep the pavement in both directions. He does not linger at doorsteps the way he once did. He eats more than he used to - at rest stops, in the van, in the evenings in front of the television - and he knows it, though he would struggle to explain exactly why the eating helps except that it occupies him in some immediate, physical way. In the evenings he eats more still, often well past the point of hunger.

He has worked hard not to think about the assault directly. He has told himself, and half-believes, that turning the memory over would undo him - that he is managing precisely because he is not looking at it. He does not know what would happen if he did, and he does not want to find out. This has meant that conversations with his wife about that night have remained thin and deflecting, and she has noticed the distance without understanding its source.

What finally brought Harold to the clinic was a moment at work three months after the assault: he froze completely outside a customer's house, unable to make himself walk up the path, and sat in the van for twenty minutes until he drove away without delivering the package. He filed it as a wrong address. He has not told his employer. He came to therapy, he said, because he does not want to lose the job, and because he is tired of feeling like a man he does not recognize. What he hopes for, quietly, is to feel trustworthy to himself again.
